A small residual validates the numerical eigenpair; a perturbation bound validates proximity to a separated population subspace under its hypotheses; neither establishes statistical consistency by itself. Consistency concerns a stated sequence of data-generating models and graph constructions as sample size grows. See von Luxburg’s tutorial and von Luxburg, Belkin, and Bousquet on consistency for the distinction.

4.5 Graph Fourier Analysis and Spectral Filtering

The same eigenbasis that supplies embedding coordinates also supplies a filtering basis. Here the object of interest is not the position of a vertex in an embedding, but the response of an operator applied to a signal. A graph signal is a quantity indexed by vertices: temperature at sensors, relevance scores on documents, or a measured attribute of people. The graph supplies the neighbourhood relation against which variation is judged. There is no required Euclidean ordering of the vertices, so adjacent labels need not be nearby in any physical or semantic space.

For a connected graph, choose orthonormal Laplacian eigenvectors 𝒖1,…,𝒖n\mathbf{u}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{u}_n. Every signal has the expansion

𝒙=∑k=1nx̂k𝒖k,x̂k=𝒖k⊤𝒙. \mathbf{x}=\sum_{k=1}^n\widehat{x}_k\mathbf{u}_k, \qquad \widehat{x}_k=\mathbf{u}_k^\top\mathbf{x}.

This is a change of coordinates, not a claim that the graph has a hidden Euclidean frequency axis. The eigenvalue orders the modes by their relative edge variation. The energy identity makes this precise:

𝒙⊤L𝒙=∑k=1nλkx̂k2. \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} =\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k\widehat{x}_k^2.

Low modes are inexpensive in the Dirichlet geometry; high modes represent rapid disagreement across edges. A measured signal may contain either. Calling a signal smooth is a modelling preference or regularisation assumption, not a fact forced by the graph.

Given a scalar function gg on the spectrum, the spectral filter is

g(L)𝒙=∑k=1ng(λk)x̂k𝒖k. g(L)\mathbf{x}=\sum_{k=1}^n g(\lambda_k)\widehat{x}_k\mathbf{u}_k.

A low-pass filter attenuates high eigenvalues and a high-pass filter emphasises them. Repeated eigenvalues cause no ambiguity in g(L)g(L): the same scalar is applied to the whole eigenspace, even though a library may return different individual basis vectors on different runs. The heat kernel, gt(λ)=exp⁡(−tλ)g_t(\lambda)=\exp(-t\lambda), gives the diffusion solution already seen above. Its scale parameter is not universal: multiplying every edge weight multiplies LL and changes the effective time scale.

Polynomial filters avoid a full eigendecomposition. If p(λ)=∑r=0Rarλrp(\lambda)=\sum_{r=0}^R a_r\lambda^r, then

p(L)𝒙=∑r=0RarLr𝒙. p(L)\mathbf{x}=\sum_{r=0}^R a_rL^r\mathbf{x}.

For a sparse graph, each multiplication by LL is a local edge operation, and the support of Lr𝒙L^r\mathbf{x} reaches at most rr graph hops from the initial support. Chebyshev polynomials are a practical way to approximate a desired response, but their spectral interval must match the chosen operator. The normalised Laplacian has eigenvalues in [0,2][0,2] under the stated convention; the unnormalised Laplacian generally does not.

Filter choice should follow the meaning of the signal. Heat filtering is natural when the signal is expected to diffuse over a time scale. Tikhonov filtering is natural when the output balances fidelity to noisy observations against edge disagreement. An ideal low-pass filter is useful as a conceptual projector but is sharp in the spectrum and can create long-range effects in the vertex domain. A polynomial approximation is useful when repeated sparse matrix-vector products are cheaper than eigenvectors, but its coefficients and scaling must be reported because two filters with the same name can have different responses.

The vertex-domain interpretation is equally important. A polynomial of degree rr cannot propagate a signal more than rr graph hops in a sparse loopless graph, although different paths can combine and cancellation can occur. A heat kernel has non-zero influence at every distance in exact arithmetic, with distant influence controlled by time and graph geometry. Thus “local graph filtering” can mean a finite-hop approximation or a rapidly decaying diffusion process. State which one is implemented when locality matters.

4.5.1 A Worked Smoothing Example

Consider a path of three vertices with unit weights and observed values 𝒚=(0,10,0)⊤\mathbf{y}=(0,10,0)^\top. The central value disagrees with both neighbours, so

𝒚⊤L𝒚=(10−0)2+(0−10)2=200. \mathbf{y}^\top L\mathbf{y} =(10-0)^2+(0-10)^2=200.

The penalised estimate

𝒙̂=arg min𝒙{∥𝒙−𝒚∥22+τ𝒙⊤L𝒙} \widehat{\mathbf{x}}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}} \{\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2+\tau\mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x}\}

satisfies (I+τL)𝒙̂=𝒚(I+\tau L)\widehat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{y}. For τ=1\tau=1, I+LI+L is

(2−10−13−10−12), \begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&3&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix},

and symmetry gives 𝒙̂=(a,b,a)⊤\widehat{\mathbf{x}}=(a,b,a)^\top with 2a−b=02a-b=0 and −2a+3b=10-2a+3b=10. Thus a=5/2a=5/2 and b=5b=5. The estimate retains the broad peak but removes the edge disagreement. Increasing τ\tau moves the solution towards a constant; decreasing it preserves more of the observation. This is a transparent example of the bias-variance choice hidden in a graph smoothness prior.

The same calculation can be interpreted as interpolation or semi-supervised learning when some entries are fixed labels. If a connected component has no labelled vertex, the minimum-energy extension is not identified by the labels: an arbitrary componentwise constant adds no edge penalty. Components and isolates should therefore be checked before fitting a graph-based predictor.

The graph neural-network analogy should be used carefully. Repeated neighbour aggregation often creates a low-pass tendency, sometimes called oversmoothing, but the exact response depends on weights, normalisation, non-linearities, residual paths, and the training objective. A spectral filter is an explicit linear operator; message passing need not be.

The figure is generated by generate_figures.py from the displayed filter responses. It illustrates the response of an operator, not the distribution of eigenvalues in a particular data set.

5 Electrical Networks, Resistance, and Spanning Trees

Interpret every edge {i,j}\{i,j\} as a resistor with conductance wijw_{ij}, hence resistance 1wij\frac{1}{w_{ij}}. Assign a potential viv_i to each vertex. Ohm’s law gives the current from ii to jj as

Iij=wij(vi−vj). I_{ij}=w_{ij}(v_i-v_j).

The net current injected at vertex ii is

∑jwij(vi−vj)=(L𝒗)i. \sum_jw_{ij}(v_i-v_j)=(L\mathbf{v})_i.

If 𝒃\mathbf{b} records external injections, Kirchhoff’s current law is L𝒗=𝒃L\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}. On a connected graph, a feasible injection vector must satisfy 𝟏⊤𝒃=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{b}=0, and potentials are determined only up to an additive constant. Adding a constant changes no voltage difference or current. Fixing one potential to zero, or imposing 𝟏⊤𝒗=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{v}=0, selects a representative.

Inject one unit at ss and remove one unit at tt, so 𝒃=𝒆s−𝒆t\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{e}_s-\mathbf{e}_t. The voltage drop vs−vtv_s-v_t is the effective resistance RstR_{st} because the imposed current is one unit. Using the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse gives the convention-independent expression

Rst=(𝒆s−𝒆t)⊤L+(𝒆s−𝒆t). R_{st}=(\mathbf{e}_s-\mathbf{e}_t)^{\top}L^+ (\mathbf{e}_s-\mathbf{e}_t).

The expression is meaningful as a finite resistance only when ss and tt are in the same connected component. Across separate components no finite unit-current solution exists, and the physical resistance is infinite. A pseudoinverse calculation should therefore be preceded by a component check rather than interpreted blindly.

The dissipated power is

ℰ(𝒗)=∑{i,j}∈Ewij(vi−vj)2=𝒗⊤L𝒗. \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{v})=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(v_i-v_j)^2=\mathbf{v}^{\top}L\mathbf{v}.

For a unit injection, power equals current times voltage drop, so ℰ(𝒗)=Rst\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{v})=R_{st}. This leads to two complementary variational principles. Among all unit flows from ss to tt, the physical current minimises total energy — Thomson’s principle. Among all potentials with vs=1v_s=1 and vt=0v_t=0, the harmonic potential minimises the Dirichlet energy subject to those boundary values — Dirichlet’s principle. These principles are developed in Doyle and Snell’s treatment of electrical networks; the finite-dimensional minimisation can also be derived directly from the positive semidefiniteness of LL.

The principles explain series and parallel laws. In series, the same current crosses each edge, so energy adds and resistances add. In parallel, a fixed voltage drop is shared, currents add, and conductances add. On the unit path 1−2−31-2-3, two unit resistors give R13=2R_{13}=2. On the unit triangle between 1 and 2, the direct edge has conductance 1 and the two-edge path has equivalent conductance 1/21/2, so the total conductance is 3/23/2 and the resistance is 2/32/3.

The variational form is often more useful than the circuit analogy itself. To calculate RstR_{st}, impose a unit potential difference between ss and tt and minimise the energy over all other vertex potentials. The minimiser is harmonic at every interior vertex because changing one potential in either direction would otherwise reduce the energy. The minimum energy is the effective conductance, so the reciprocal is the effective resistance. This formulation extends immediately to a graph whose edges are similarity weights, provided the report says that resistance is a structural quantity in the similarity geometry rather than a literal physical resistance.

Grounding is a coordinate choice, not a change to the network. Delete row and column rr from a connected Laplacian, solve the positive-definite reduced system, and set vr=0v_r=0. If a different vertex is grounded, every potential changes by a constant but every difference and current remains the same. A pseudoinverse returns the centred representative instead. These solutions should agree on voltage differences; comparing the full vectors without accounting for the gauge can make identical physical solutions look different.

For multiple right-hand sides, factorisation and solve costs should be separated. A sparse direct factorisation may be expensive once but efficient for many injections. An iterative method may have low setup cost but require a strong preconditioner to solve many related systems. A spectral sparsifier can reduce the cost of repeated multiplication or act as a preconditioner while preserving the energy geometry approximately. The appropriate choice depends on whether the analysis needs one resistance query, an all-pairs approximation, many boundary-value solves, or a repeated time evolution.

Resistance is a metric on the vertices of a connected graph, called effective-resistance distance, although it is not the same as shortest-path distance. The triangle example makes the distinction concrete: the shortest-path distance between adjacent vertices is 1, while the effective resistance is 2/32/3 because an alternative route reduces the response to a unit injection. Doyle and Snell provide the standard electrical-network background for this interpretation.

5.1 Spanning Trees and Resistance

A spanning tree is a connected, acyclic subgraph containing every vertex. If edge weights are conductances, assign a tree TT weight

w(T)=∏e∈Twe. w(T)=\prod_{e\in T}w_e.

The weighted matrix-tree theorem states that any principal cofactor of LL equals

∑T spanning treew(T). \sum_{T\text{ spanning tree}}w(T).

For an unweighted graph this is the number of spanning trees. A cofactor is obtained by deleting the same one row and column from LL.

The theorem is not an isolated determinant trick. It connects the Laplacian spectrum, electrical response, and random spanning trees. If a weighted spanning tree is sampled with probability proportional to w(T)w(T), then the probability that edge ee is present is

Pr⁡(e∈T)=weRe, \Pr(e\in T)=w_eR_e,

where ReR_e is the effective resistance between the endpoints of ee. This quantity lies between zero and one: a high-conductance edge can still have low inclusion probability if many redundant routes make it unnecessary, while a bridge has Re=1/weR_e=1/w_e and is present with probability one. The edge-marginal result is part of the effective-resistance framework developed by Spielman and Srivastava; edge events are not independent.

5.1.1 Triangle Check

The unweighted triangle has three spanning trees, one for each choice of the omitted edge. Its Laplacian is

L=(2−1−1−12−1−1−12). L=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&-1\\-1&2&-1\\-1&-1&2\end{pmatrix}.

Deleting the third row and column leaves a 22 by 22 matrix with determinant 33, matching the three trees. For any edge, we=1w_e=1 and the endpoint resistance is 2/32/3, so the marginal inclusion probability is 2/32/3. Summing the three marginals gives 22, the number of edges in every spanning tree on three vertices. This last equality is a useful sanity check, but it does not establish independence: the sampled tree always contains exactly two edges.

The same edge-marginal identity gives a useful interpretation of resistance. An edge has high resistance when its endpoints are difficult to connect through the rest of the network, so it is structurally important to a random spanning tree. An edge with low resistance is replaceable by many alternative paths. This interpretation is probabilistic and global; it should not be confused with the local resistance 1/we1/w_e of the edge considered in isolation.

Resistance also links directly to random-walk time. For a connected undirected graph with total volume MM, the expected commute time from ss to tt and back is

𝔼s[Tt]+𝔼t[Ts]=MRst. \mathbb{E}_s[T_t]+\mathbb{E}_t[T_s]=M R_{st}.

The identity explains why a high-resistance pair is hard to traverse in both directions on average, but it does not say that every one-way hitting time is large in the same way. The two directed hitting times can be very unequal when degrees differ; only their sum is fixed by the resistance identity. In the unit path 1−2−31-2-3, M=4M=4 and R13=2R_{13}=2, so the commute time is eight steps. A direct edge added between the endpoints lowers resistance and therefore lowers the round-trip time, even though the original shortest path was already only two edges.

The electrical and walk views also clarify scaling. If all conductances are multiplied by cc, a discrete walk is unchanged because each transition ratio is unchanged, while physical resistance is divided by cc and volume is multiplied by cc. Their product, and hence discrete commute time, is unchanged. Continuous-time diffusion with generator −L-L is different: its rates are multiplied by cc, so the same physical evolution occurs on a clock accelerated by cc. Confusing these clocks is a common source of incorrect comparisons between simulations and formulas.

5.2 What the Analogy Does and Does Not Preserve

The walk, diffusion, and network descriptions agree because they are built from the same symmetric conductance matrix. The stationary measure is degree volume, the Laplacian energy is expected squared voltage disagreement under a stationary edge traversal, hitting times solve grounded Laplacian systems, commute times equal volume times resistance, and spanning-tree weights are Laplacian cofactors. These are linked statements, not interchangeable definitions.

Several convention changes break a careless transfer. Multiplying all conductances by c>0c>0 leaves PP and π\pi unchanged, because both numerator and degree scale by cc, but multiplies LL by cc, divides physical resistances by cc, and therefore leaves the discrete commute time MRstMR_{st} unchanged because MM also scales by cc. Continuous-time diffusion with generator −L-L does change speed under this scaling: its clock runs cc times as fast. A statement about “time” must therefore specify discrete steps or the continuous-time generator.

Disconnected graphs require componentwise statements. The stationary distribution is not unique across components, a walk cannot hit a target in another component, and LL has one zero mode per component. Isolated vertices require an explicit convention for D−1/2D^{-1/2} and for the normalised Laplacian. Directed graphs need not be reversible and generally require a different stationary analysis; the symmetric electrical analogy does not transfer merely because a directed adjacency matrix exists.

Finally, a numerical result should preserve the model choices that make the identities testable. Record whether parallel edges were summed, whether self-loops were retained, whether a route network was symmetrised, and whether weights mean conductance, similarity, count, or distance. Check L𝟏=0L\mathbf{1}=0, the component count, the energy identity, and a small resistance or hitting-time calculation before trusting a large eigensolve. The most common failure is not a difficult theorem; it is applying a correct theorem to a matrix whose rows, weights, or normalisation represent a different object.

6 Worked Graph Laboratories

The following calculations are deliberately explicit. They can be used as unit tests for a graph library and as figures in the primer. All graphs below are unweighted unless an edge weight is displayed.

6.1 The Path: Boundary Conditions Matter

The earlier path calculations checked the operator and bounded one eigenvalue. This revisit adds the whole graph family’s spectrum, exposing how endpoint boundary conditions and graph size affect the low modes. For the path PnP_n, the combinatorial Laplacian is tridiagonal with endpoint diagonal entries one, interior diagonal entries two, and −1-1 on neighbouring off-diagonals. Its eigenvalues are

λk(L)=2−2cos⁡(πkn),k=0,1,…,n−1. \lambda_k(L)=2-2\cos\left(\frac{\pi k}{n}\right), \qquad k=0,1,\ldots,n-1.

The k=0k=0 mode is constant. For P4P_4, the spectrum is 0,2−2,2,2+20,2-\sqrt2,2,2+\sqrt2, so λ2=2−2≈0.585786\lambda_2=2-\sqrt2\approx0.585786. The trial vector x=(3,1,−1,−3)⊤x=(3,1,-1,-3)^{\top} gives RL(x)=3/5=0.6R_L(x)=3/5=0.6, a valid upper bound but not the exact eigenvalue.

For P4P_4, the cut after vertex two has boundary one and both sides have volume three, so ϕ=13\phi=\frac{1}{3}. A singleton endpoint has boundary one and volume one, so its conductance is one. The balanced cut is therefore the relevant one for conductance. The normalised spectrum is

νk=1−cos⁡(πkn−1),k=0,1,…,n−1, \nu_k=1-\cos\left(\frac{\pi k}{n-1}\right), \qquad k=0,1,\ldots,n-1,

under the positive-degree convention. For P4P_4 this is 0,12,32,20,\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},2. The combinatorial and normalised second eigenvalues are close enough to invite confusion, but they have different units and different eigenvectors.

6.2 The Cycle: Fourier Modes and No Boundary Endpoints

For the cycle CnC_n, each vertex has degree two and the adjacency eigenvectors are discrete Fourier modes. The real Laplacian eigenvalues are

λk(L)=2−2cos⁡(2πkn),k=0,1,…,n−1. \lambda_k(L)=2-2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{n}\right), \qquad k=0,1,\ldots,n-1.

Because the graph is regular, the normalised values are νk=λk/2\nu_k=\lambda_k/2 and the adjacency values are αk=2cos⁡(2πk/n)\alpha_k=2\cos(2\pi k/n). For C4C_4 the adjacency spectrum is (2,0,0,−2)(2,0,0,-2). The eigenvalue −2-2 gives the alternating mode and explains the period-two ordinary walk; a positive top gap alone does not guarantee convergence without laziness.

For an even cycle, a contiguous set of n/2n/2 vertices has two boundary edges and volume nn, giving conductance 2/n2/n. Any non-empty proper set with more than one interval has at least as much boundary for its volume, so this contiguous balanced cut is optimal. The cycle’s low modes vary smoothly around the ring, while the path’s endpoint boundary changes the eigenfunctions. A plot should show the first non-constant mode on the vertex order around the cycle, not an arbitrary force-directed layout.

6.3 The Star: Degree Bias Is Not a Numerical Detail

Let SnS_n have centre 00 and leaves 1,…,n−11,\ldots,n-1. Its combinatorial Laplacian is

L=(n−1−1−1⋯−1−110⋯0−101⋯0⋮⋮⋮⋱⋮−100⋯1). L= \begin{pmatrix} n-1&-1&-1&\cdots&-1\\ -1&1&0&\cdots&0\\ -1&0&1&\cdots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ -1&0&0&\cdots&1 \end{pmatrix}.

There are three invariant types of vector. The constant vector has eigenvalue zero. A leaf-contrast vector with centre value zero and leaf values summing to zero has eigenvalue one; this space has dimension n−2n-2. The remaining vector, constant on the leaves and opposite at the centre, has eigenvalue nn. Thus

spec⁡(L)={0,1(n−2),n}. \operatorname{spec}(L)=\{0,1^{(n-2)},n\}.

The symmetric normalised adjacency has centre-to-leaf entries 1/n−11/\sqrt{n-1} and no other off-diagonal entries. Its eigenvalues are 1,−1,0(n−2)1,-1,0^{(n-2)}, so

spec⁡(ℒ)={0,2,1(n−2)}. \operatorname{spec}(\mathcal{L})=\{0,2,1^{(n-2)}\}.

The combinatorial second eigenvalue is one regardless of the number of leaves, whereas the normalised second eigenvalue is also one but lives in a different coordinate geometry. A singleton leaf has b=1b=1 and volume one, hence ϕ=1\phi=1. A set containing the centre and kk leaves has boundary n−1−kn-1-k; its complement has exactly that volume, so its conductance is also one. The star has no low-conductance volume bottleneck despite its poor ordinary vertex-to-vertex geometry. This is why a small algebraic connectivity should not be described as a universal measure of vertex-removal resilience.

6.4 The Clique: Expansion Without a Preferred Direction

For the complete graph KnK_n, every vertex has degree n−1n-1 and

A=J−I,L=nI−J. A=J-I,\qquad L=nI-J.

The constant vector has eigenvalue zero and every mean-zero vector has eigenvalue nn. The non-zero eigenspace is (n−1)(n-1)-fold degenerate. Individual eigenvectors returned by a numerical routine have no graph-intrinsic meaning; the projector onto the mean-zero space is the invariant object.

For a set of size s≤n/2s\leq n/2, b(S)=s(n−s)b(S)=s(n-s) and vol⁡(S)=s(n−1)\operatorname{vol}(S)=s(n-1). Hence

ϕ(S)=n−sn−1,Ncut⁡(S)=nn−1. \phi(S)=\frac{n-s}{n-1}, \qquad \operatorname{Ncut}(S)=\frac{n}{n-1}.

Every cut has the same normalised-cut value, although conductance is smallest for the most balanced cut. This is a useful warning: a relaxed objective can be degenerate even when the graph is maximally connected. A clustering routine fed only the clique’s non-zero eigenspace must obtain its labels from an extra criterion or from numerical accident.

6.5 Two Triangles Joined by a Weak Bridge

We now turn the opening’s weak-bridge mechanism into an explicit cut and variational bound, then derive the exact eigenvalue and record its sensitivity to the bridge weight. Take triangles AA and BB, join one vertex in each by an edge of weight ε>0\varepsilon>0, and leave all other triangle edges at weight one. The graph is connected for every positive ε\varepsilon, so LL has one zero eigenvalue. The cut separating the triangles has boundary ε\varepsilon and each side has volume 6+ε6+\varepsilon. Therefore

ϕ(A)=ε6+ε,Ncut⁡(A)=2ε6+ε. \phi(A)=\frac{\varepsilon}{6+\varepsilon}, \qquad \operatorname{Ncut}(A)=\frac{2\varepsilon}{6+\varepsilon}.

Take the trial vector equal to +1+1 on AA and −1-1 on BB. Its only non-zero edge difference is across the bridge, so

x⊤Lxx⊤x=4ε6=2ε3. \frac{x^{\top}Lx}{x^{\top}x} =\frac{4\varepsilon}{6}=\frac{2\varepsilon}{3}.

This is an upper bound on the combinatorial λ2\lambda_2. For the normalised quotient, the degree-weighted norm is 12+2ε12+2\varepsilon and the energy is 4ε4\varepsilon, giving

ν2≤4ε12+2ε=2ε6+ε=Ncut⁡(A). \nu_2\leq\frac{4\varepsilon}{12+2\varepsilon} =\frac{2\varepsilon}{6+\varepsilon} =\operatorname{Ncut}(A).

The equality at the end is expected: the trial vector is exactly the centred two-valued indicator for this equal-volume cut. It does not prove that the second eigenvalue equals this value, because the bridge endpoints can adjust their values and lower the energy further. It does prove the correct scaling: as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow0, the spectral gap is at most linear in the bridge weight. The component count changes discontinuously at ε=0\varepsilon=0, whereas the gap records the continuous approach to disconnection.

This example is also a unit test for weight semantics. Replacing the one bridge by two parallel edges of weights ε1\varepsilon_1 and ε2\varepsilon_2 gives the same Laplacian as one aggregated edge of weight ε1+ε2\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2. Treating a distance as that weight reverses the intended effect: a longer distance would strengthen the coupling. A similarity map such as w=exp⁡(−d2/(2σ2))w=\exp(-d^2/(2\sigma^2)) is an additional modelling decision, not a spectral identity.

The curves are generated from the six-vertex weighted graph in generate_figures.py. The logarithmic horizontal axis makes the continuous approach to disconnection visible across several orders of magnitude.

6.5.1 An Exact Weak-Bridge Eigenvalue

The preceding weak-bridge calculation supplied an upper bound. Here we calculate the eigenvalue itself and identify the adjustment that makes the bound strict. Let AA and BB be triangles, let their bridge endpoints have values aa and −a-a, and let the other two vertices in each triangle have values bb and −b-b. This antisymmetric subspace is invariant under the Laplacian. The bridge endpoint receives the two internal triangle contributions and the weighted bridge contribution, so its eigen-equation is

λa=(2+2ε)a−2b. \lambda a=(2+2\varepsilon)a-2b.

At a non-bridge triangle vertex, the eigen-equation is

λb=b−a. \lambda b=b-a.

The determinant condition is therefore

∣2+2ε−λ−2−11−λ∣=0,λ2−(3+2ε)λ+2ε=0. \begin{vmatrix} 2+2\varepsilon-\lambda&-2\\ -1&1-\lambda \end{vmatrix}=0, \qquad \lambda^2-(3+2\varepsilon)\lambda+2\varepsilon=0.

The smaller root is

λbridge=3+2ε−9+4ε+4ε22. \lambda_{\mathrm{bridge}} =\frac{3+2\varepsilon-\sqrt{9+4\varepsilon+4\varepsilon^2}}2.

It is the algebraic-connectivity mode for the connected graph in the weak-bridge regime. Expanding the square root at zero gives

λbridge=23ε+O(ε2). \lambda_{\mathrm{bridge}} =\frac{2}{3}\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2).

The piecewise-constant trial vector gave 2ε/32\varepsilon/3 exactly as its Rayleigh quotient, so it captures the leading scale. The exact eigenvector allows the bridge endpoints to move slightly relative to the other triangle vertices, lowering the eigenvalue at higher orders. This is a useful lesson about trial vectors: they can identify scaling and certify an upper bound without being the true mode.

The normalised operator sees the same bridge through a different denominator. The bridge endpoints have degree 2+ε2+\varepsilon, while the other vertices have degree two. The equal-sign piecewise vector remains degree-balanced by symmetry, and its quotient is

4ε12+2ε=2ε6+ε. \frac{4\varepsilon}{12+2\varepsilon} =\frac{2\varepsilon}{6+\varepsilon}.

Unlike the combinatorial calculation, the endpoint adjustment for the exact normalised eigenvector must account for the changed endpoint degrees. The important invariant is not that the two eigenvalues are numerically equal; it is that both become small linearly with the weak coupling while the graph remains mathematically connected.

6.5.2 A Perturbation Ledger for the Weak Bridge

The trial bound and exact eigenvalue above describe one bridge weight at a time. This ledger adds a parameter experiment: it records which numerical and downstream quantities change together as the bridge weight varies.

The weak-bridge graph supplies a second integrated test. At ε=0\varepsilon=0, the two triangles are disconnected and the Laplacian has two zero modes. For every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is one zero mode and a small positive bridge mode. The zero multiplicity is discontinuous at the exact deletion, while the positive eigenvalue approaches zero continuously. This is why a component count and an algebraic-connectivity value answer different robustness questions.

The perturbation ledger should record the bridge weight, component count, λ2\lambda_2, the normalised gap, the cut boundary, the cut volume, and the residual of the reported eigenpair. It should also record the eigenvector’s group means and within-group deviations. In the weak-bridge regime the group means dominate and the deviations are small; as the bridge becomes stronger, the mode ceases to be a pair of nearly constant group indicators. That transition is more informative than a single threshold saying “community” or “no community”.

The ledger also exposes scale dependence. Multiplying every edge weight by cc multiplies the combinatorial gap and divides effective resistances by cc, but leaves the random-walk matrix and normalised spectrum unchanged. Increasing only the bridge weight changes all of these quantities because it changes both connectivity and, for normalised methods, local degree. A report that lists only a normalised eigenvalue would miss the absolute conductance scale; a report that lists only λ2\lambda_2 would miss degree-relative behaviour. Preserve both when the application could plausibly depend on either.

6.6 Worked Cut Ledger for the Four-Vertex Path

The earlier sweep introduced thresholding; this revisit audits the discrete objectives for its candidate cuts. The path P4P_4 is small enough to calculate every quantity without a black-box routine. Its degrees in vertex order are (1,2,2,1)(1,2,2,1) and its total volume is M=6M=6. Consider first the endpoint cut S1={1}S_1=\{1\}. The boundary weight is one, the two volumes are one and five, and therefore

ϕ(S1)=1,Ncut⁡(S1)=1(1+15)=65. \phi(S_1)=1, \qquad \operatorname{Ncut}(S_1)=1\left(1+\frac15\right)=\frac65.

The cardinality ratio cut is also easy to calculate:

RatioCut⁡(S1)=1(1+13)=43. \operatorname{RatioCut}(S_1)=1\left(1+\frac13\right)=\frac43.

The endpoint is a poor conductance cut because its boundary is as large as the entire volume of the small side. It is not rejected because it has few vertices; it is rejected because one unit of boundary is large relative to one unit of incident weight.

Now take S2={1,2}S_2=\{1,2\}. Its boundary is still one, but both sides have volume three. Consequently,

ϕ(S2)=13,Ncut⁡(S2)=1(13+13)=23,RatioCut⁡(S2)=1(12+12)=1. \phi(S_2)=\frac13, \qquad \operatorname{Ncut}(S_2)=1\left(\frac13+\frac13\right)=\frac23, \qquad \operatorname{RatioCut}(S_2)=1\left(\frac12+\frac12\right)=1.

The degree-centred indicator for S2S_2 has values +1/2+1/2 on vertices one and two and −1/2-1/2 on vertices three and four. Its symmetric coordinate is

z=D1/2f=(12,12,−12,−12)⊤. z=D^{1/2}f =\left(\frac12,\frac1{\sqrt2},-\frac1{\sqrt2},-\frac12\right)^{\top}.

Substituting it into the normalised Rayleigh quotient gives 2/32/3, exactly the normalised-cut value. The second normalised eigenvalue is 1/21/2, so the relaxed optimum is below the best two-valued cut, as the variational argument predicts. The lower Cheeger bound gives ν2/2=1/4≤Φ=1/3\nu_2/2=1/4\leq\Phi=1/3, while the general upper bound gives Φ≤2ν2=1\Phi\leq\sqrt{2\nu_2}=1. On this tiny graph the upper constant is loose, but the lower bound has the correct order.

This ledger is also a useful check on denominators. If the endpoint cut is reported with vol⁡(S)=1\operatorname{vol}(S)=1 and the complement volume is stated as four, an edge has been counted incorrectly: the complement contains the internal edge between vertices two and three, and its total incident weight is five. The boundary is counted once; internal edges contribute twice to volume. Writing those two counting rules beside a numerical result prevents many normalised-cut discrepancies.

6.7 A Fully Worked Three-Vertex Filter

The heat and Tikhonov examples evaluated particular smoothing operators. This revisit exposes the signal’s modal coefficients so that we can compare several filter responses on exactly the same input. Take the unit path P3P_3 and the observation y=(0,10,0)⊤y=(0,10,0)^{\top}. The Laplacian eigenvectors can be chosen as

u0=13(1,1,1)⊤,u1=12(1,0,−1)⊤,u2=16(1,−2,1)⊤, u_0=\frac1{\sqrt3}(1,1,1)^{\top},\quad u_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,-1)^{\top},\quad u_2=\frac1{\sqrt6}(1,-2,1)^{\top},

with eigenvalues 00, 11, and 33. The observation is symmetric, so its coefficient on the antisymmetric mode is zero. The other coefficients are

ŷ0=u0⊤y=103,ŷ2=u2⊤y=−206. \widehat y_0=u_0^{\top}y=\frac{10}{\sqrt3}, \qquad \widehat y_2=u_2^{\top}y=-\frac{20}{\sqrt6}.

For heat time t=1t=1, the filtered coefficients are x̂0=10/3\widehat x_0=10/\sqrt3 and x̂2=−20e−3/6\widehat x_2=-20e^{-3}/\sqrt6. Reconstructing gives

xheat(1)=103(1,1,1)⊤−10e−33(1,−2,1)⊤. x_{\mathrm{heat}}(1) =\frac{10}{3}(1,1,1)^{\top} -\frac{10e^{-3}}3(1,-2,1)^{\top}.

The central value is therefore 10/3+20e−3/310/3+20e^{-3}/3, and each endpoint is 10/3−10e−3/310/3-10e^{-3}/3. Heat filtering retains the ordinary mean and substantially reduces the isolated high-frequency peak.

For Tikhonov smoothing with τ=1\tau=1, the high-mode coefficient is multiplied by 1/(1+3)=1/41/(1+3)=1/4. Thus

xTik=103(1,1,1)⊤−56(1,−2,1)⊤=(52,5,52)⊤. x_{\mathrm{Tik}} =\frac{10}{3}(1,1,1)^{\top} -\frac56(1,-2,1)^{\top} =\left(\frac52,5,\frac52\right)^{\top}.

This result can also be checked directly. The first-order system is

(2−10−13−10−12)(aba)=(0100), \begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&3&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}a\\b\\a\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}0\\10\\0\end{pmatrix},

so 2a−b=02a-b=0 and −2a+3b=10-2a+3b=10, which give a=5/2a=5/2 and b=5b=5. The modal calculation therefore agrees with the vertex-domain solve and makes the different attenuation factors explicit.

The two filters make the same qualitative choice but not the same numerical choice. At λ=3\lambda=3, heat at unit time multiplies by e−3≈0.0498e^{-3}\approx0.0498, whereas Tikhonov at unit strength multiplies by 1/41/4. A figure that compares them should label the parameter values rather than calling both settings “one step”.

6.8 What the Derivations Do Not Prove

The inequalities connect graph quantities, but they do not remove the need for model validation. A small ν2\nu_2 proves that some degree-weighted signal varies slowly across the graph. It does not identify the cause of that slow variation. The cause may be a meaningful community, a duplicated identifier, an omitted edge, or a weight convention that turned distance into similarity. The theorem is about the supplied weighted graph; the scientific interpretation needs an additional argument.

The conductance guarantee also concerns a particular graph and its volume measure. If a similarity graph is rebuilt after changing a nearest-neighbour parameter, the guarantee applies separately to each new graph. Comparing the two resulting eigenvalues without recording the changes in component count, degree distribution, and weight scale confounds spectral sensitivity with graph construction sensitivity. A useful robustness table should include the edge rule, number of vertices and edges, number of components, total volume, target eigenvalue, residual, sweep conductance, and the overlap of the resulting partition with the reference partition.

There is a second distinction between theorem and computation. An exact zero eigenvalue corresponds to a component in exact arithmetic, but a floating-point solver reports a small number. The decision threshold should be tied to a matrix norm and a residual, not copied from a different graph. A weak bridge can generate a small positive eigenvalue, while a disconnected graph can generate a numerically tiny value that is exactly zero in the mathematical model. Run a component algorithm on the edge data before deciding how many eigenvectors to request.

Finally, a repeated eigenvalue makes individual coordinates non-identifiable. The clique’s mean-zero eigenspace is the clearest example, but nearly repeated eigenvalues occur in many symmetric or weakly perturbed graphs. Compare the projectors QQ⊤QQ^{\top} for the selected subspaces, or compare downstream invariants such as pairwise embedding distances and cut values. A sign flip of one eigenvector is harmless; a rotation within a repeated eigenspace is also harmless, but it can make a column-by-column comparison look unstable. This validation rule is part of the expansion argument because a claimed community boundary is a property of the rounded subspace, not of an arbitrary basis returned by one eigensolver. ### A Compact Portfolio of Small Graphs

This portfolio is a reference synthesis of the preceding laboratories. Its new task is to assemble their results into a regression suite: which graph tests boundary effects, degree bias, degeneracy, or sensitivity? The family descriptions below recall the mechanisms rather than introduce additional derivations.

On the path PnP_n, a low-frequency mode changes gradually from one endpoint to the other. Its small second eigenvalue reflects the single-dimensional bottleneck: removing any interior edge disconnects the graph. On the cycle CnC_n, there are two directions around the ring, so the same-scale variation can spread in either direction. The cycle’s Laplacian eigenvectors can be chosen as discrete sine and cosine waves, making it the closest elementary analogue of a periodic Fourier domain. The complete graph KnK_n has no sparse geometric bottleneck. Its Laplacian is nI−JnI-J, with eigenvalue 00 on constants and eigenvalue nn on every mean-zero vector. The repeated non-zero eigenvalue means that no particular mean-zero direction is preferred by the graph.

These examples separate geometry from degree. A path and a cycle can have similar local degrees but different global routes. A complete graph has very high connectivity, yet its non-constant eigenspace is maximally degenerate. Consequently, a stable eigenvalue can coexist with unstable individual eigenvectors when multiplicity is present.

The star SnS_n has one central vertex joined to n−1n-1 leaves. Its combinatorial Laplacian has eigenvalues 00, 11 with multiplicity n−2n-2, and nn. A signal that changes between leaves can have the same energy regardless of which leaf-to-leaf contrast is selected; the graph sees all leaves symmetrically. The normalised operator changes the coordinates because the hub has degree n−1n-1 while each leaf has degree one. This is a compact warning against interpreting an unnormalised embedding as if every vertex had equal exposure.

For a random walk, the hub is visited more often in stationarity than an individual leaf, but the walk leaves it immediately in an unweighted star. The stationary distribution and the one-step dynamics therefore tell different stories: degree controls equilibrium mass, while the transition row controls local persistence.

Take two triangles and join one vertex in each by an edge of weight ε\varepsilon. For every ε>0\varepsilon>0 the graph is connected, so the combinatorial Laplacian has exactly one zero eigenvalue. As ε\varepsilon decreases, the second eigenvalue approaches zero because the vector that is approximately constant and opposite on the two triangles pays energy mainly on the bridge. The corresponding normalised eigenvector supplies a natural two-way cut. The example demonstrates why a component count alone is a weak robustness summary: it cannot distinguish a strong connection from an almost severed one.

The same graph gives a controlled sensitivity experiment. Replace the bridge by two parallel edges, aggregate them into one weight, and compare with a single edge of the same total weight. The Laplacian is unchanged if the parallel weights are summed. Replace the edge by a distance and use that distance directly as a weight, however, and the model changes direction: a longer “connection” would become stronger. Similarity transformations such as w=exp⁡(−d2/(2σ2))w=\exp(-d^2/(2\sigma^2)) are modelling choices that should be reported.

The spectra show why graph families with similar vertex counts can have very different low modes and why the clique’s repeated non-zero eigenvalue leaves no preferred direction inside its mean-zero eigenspace.

The path checks boundary effects, the cycle checks periodic modes, the clique checks degeneracy, the star checks degree normalisation, and the weak bridge checks quantitative connectivity. A compact regression suite can assert the following without relying on a particular eigenvector sign:

  • the number of Laplacian zeros agrees with the component count;
  • the sorted eigenvalues are non-negative up to numerical tolerance;
  • L𝟏=0L\mathbf{1}=0 and the trace equals twice total edge weight;
  • a repeated eigenspace is compared by a projector or residual, not by a named individual vector;
  • rescaling all weights rescales LL but leaves PP unchanged; and
  • a normalised Laplacian has spectrum in the stated interval under the chosen isolate convention.

These tests are small enough to run in both Python and R. They belong beside the analysis rather than in an informal notebook because they encode the operator contract on which every later interpretation depends.

6.9 One Graph Through Five Spectral Lenses

This revisit translates between operators while holding the original four-vertex laboratory fixed: a three-vertex path and one isolate. Its purpose is to test consistency across interpretations, after the earlier laboratories tested individual calculations.

Ask five different questions of that three-vertex path and isolate. The combinatorial Laplacian says that the path component has two positive internal modes and that the isolate contributes an additional null direction. The normalised Laplacian says how those modes change when the path’s higher-degree centre is accounted for. The random walk says that the isolate has no transition rule until one is specified and that the path’s ordinary walk alternates between bipartite sides. Heat diffusion says that a signal on the path smooths towards its component mean while the isolate retains its own value. The electrical model says that no current can cross from the path to the isolate.

These are not five unrelated analyses. They are five questions asked of the same edge relation, with different state spaces, normalisations, and time interpretations. The shared Laplacian energy explains why the answers are related, while the differences explain why a result should not be copied from one view into another without translation. For example, a degree-weighted stationary limit is appropriate for a random-walk function but is not the ordinary mean of combinatorial heat. A normalised eigenvalue in [0,2][0,2] cannot be compared numerically with a combinatorial eigenvalue whose units are the edge weights.

This single-graph exercise is a useful pre-flight check for an applied analysis. Write down what a vertex value means, what an edge weight means, and what conservation law or objective the operator should respect. Then calculate one invariant for each interpretation: component count, energy, stationary mass, conserved sum, or residual. If the implementation cannot explain these small answers, a large graph result is not ready for interpretation.

7 What Problems Spectral Methods Solve

Spectral graph theory is useful when the important structure is relational and global rather than attached to individual rows of a data table. The following use cases are deliberately stated as problem formulations, because the same algorithm can be appropriate in one setting and misleading in another.

7.1 Community Detection and Network Segmentation

Suppose a network contains dense groups connected by relatively few edges. A community-detection task asks for a partition whose within-group connections are strong relative to its boundary. The combinatorial Laplacian sees a weak bridge through a small energy cost, while the normalised Laplacian prevents a large-volume group from winning solely because it has more edges. The second normalised eigenvector gives a continuous ordering; a sweep turns that ordering into a candidate cut, and several eigenvectors can be rounded into multiple groups.

The method solves a relaxation problem, not an oracle-labelled classification problem. It is valuable when the researcher can defend the similarity graph and wants a global partition objective with a certificate such as conductance. It is less suitable when communities are defined by metadata that was never encoded in the edges, or when direction, signed interaction, or temporal order is the scientific signal. Report the graph-construction rule, the operator, the number of modes, the rounding rule, and the sensitivity of the partition to each of them.

For a practical comparison, take a social graph with two dense groups and one high-degree hub that links to both. Raw degree does not identify the groups; the hub may be the most important vertex by centrality while being unhelpful as a boundary marker. A normalised spectral embedding can place the two groups apart while keeping the hub near the interface. If the hub is instead a data integration artefact caused by duplicated identifiers, no choice of eigenvalue solver fixes the problem. The distinction between structural ambiguity and numerical error is central to a defensible result.

The same reasoning applies to document, biological, and transaction graphs, but the edge semantics change the claim. A document graph built from cosine similarity asks which documents have similar observed features. A protein-interaction graph asks which recorded interactions are connected, often with substantial uncertainty about missing edges. A transaction graph can encode repeated activity, but high weight may then reflect exposure or reporting intensity rather than affinity. Spectral clustering does not remove these differences; it makes them visible through the energy being optimised.

Use the two-triangle bridge as a controlled benchmark before interpreting a data-derived partition. Let the internal triangle edges have weight one and the bridge have weight ε\varepsilon. A vector that is nearly constant on each triangle pays little energy inside either group and pays approximately 4ε4\varepsilon across the bridge when the two group levels differ by two. Its Rayleigh quotient therefore decreases with ε\varepsilon, which explains why the low mode separates the triangles. The calculation demonstrates a mechanism, not a universal community law: a graph with several comparable bridges, heterogeneous degree, or overlapping groups can produce a rotated or unstable low-dimensional subspace.

For more than two groups, the first kk non-trivial modes form an embedding rather than a partition. The rows of the embedding can be clustered, but that second clustering step introduces its own distance, scaling, and number-of-clusters choices. A useful report gives the eigenvalue gaps, the embedding dimension, the rounding method, the cut or modularity-like score used for comparison, and the stability under resampling or edge perturbation. If the graph has an exact component structure, component labels should be reported before any spectral clustering result because the first modes may reproduce that structure.

The number of groups is not supplied by the Laplacian automatically. A visible gap after the first few eigenvalues can motivate an embedding dimension, but the gap can disappear when the similarity bandwidth or edge threshold changes. Compare candidate dimensions against a downstream objective and against stability. If the result is exploratory, show several plausible dimensions; if it drives an allocation, pre-specify the rounding rule and report how the allocation changes under the alternatives.

A useful graphical workflow is to calculate the cut first, then add its result to the graph. An igraph object can carry component, degree, and spectral_value vertex attributes; as_tbl_graph() and activate(nodes) can make those attributes available for tidy summaries and ggraph aesthetics. Keep a separate cut ledger containing threshold, side volume, boundary weight, conductance, and vertex count. The ledger is more auditable than a plot, while the plot can show which vertices and edges the selected threshold contains.

If a repeated eigenvalue means that the embedding can rotate, do not interpret one coordinate as a discovered axis. Compare pairwise distances in the embedding, the projector onto the selected eigenspace, or the stability of the rounded partition. A sign flip is harmless; a rotation within a repeated eigenspace is not a numerical error. This is why a clique belongs in the laboratory: its repeated eigenvalue makes non-uniqueness visible before it appears in a large data set.

7.2 Semi-Supervised Learning and Signal Completion

Graph-based learning uses a small set of labelled vertices to infer labels or values on unlabelled vertices. The smoothness prior says that strongly linked vertices should have similar predictions. In its simplest form, labelled values are fixed and unlabelled values minimise the Dirichlet energy. The first-order condition on every unlabelled vertex is harmonicity:

(L𝒙)i=0,i unlabelled. (L\mathbf{x})_i=0, \qquad i\text{ unlabelled}.

This solves a concrete missing-information problem when the graph captures which observations should borrow strength from one another. It also exposes two failure modes. A graph component with no label has an undetermined componentwise constant. A weak or incorrect bridge transmits a label across a boundary that should have been preserved. Component counts, bridge weights, and held-out labels should therefore be part of validation.

The same framework supports graph-regularised regression. Given observations 𝒚\mathbf{y}, minimise a data-fit term plus τ𝒙⊤L𝒙\tau\mathbf{x}^{\top}L\mathbf{x}. The parameter τ\tau controls how much the model trusts relational smoothness, while the edge weights decide where that smoothness is imposed. Cross-validation can choose τ\tau for prediction, but it cannot by itself validate that the edge semantics are scientifically meaningful.

The harmonic calculation is worth deriving because it gives a direct interpretation of the matrix blocks. Partition the vertices into labelled set LL and unlabelled set UU, and write the Laplacian in the corresponding order. Fixing 𝒙L\mathbf{x}_L leaves the unlabelled objective

12𝒙U⊤LUU𝒙U+𝒙U⊤LUL𝒙Lconstant. \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}_U^{\top}L_{UU}\mathbf{x}_U +\mathbf{x}_U^{\top}L_{UL}\mathbf{x}_L \text{constant}.

Differentiating gives LUU𝒙U=−LUL𝒙LL_{UU}\mathbf{x}_U=-L_{UL}\mathbf{x}_L. If every connected component contains a labelled vertex, LUUL_{UU} is positive definite and the solution is unique. At an unlabelled vertex the equation is a weighted average of neighbouring values, so the algebra and the intuitive “smooth interpolation” story agree. If a component has no label, its block retains a constant null direction and no amount of numerical precision identifies an absolute prediction there.

This model also clarifies what a validation set must test. A low-energy prediction may be deliberately wrong when labels change sharply across a strong edge. Hold out labels within each component, compare against a non-graph baseline, and vary the graph bandwidth, neighbourhood size, and weight transform. If performance changes substantially under plausible graph constructions, the graph is acting as an influential prior and the uncertainty should be reported as model sensitivity rather than hidden in a single selected spectrum.

For a six-vertex path, suppose the first and last vertices have fixed values 1 and 0. The unlabelled solution is a linear interpolation, because every interior vertex has zero Laplacian residual. If the middle edge is weakened, the interpolation develops a sharper change there: the graph is saying that the two sides are less obliged to agree. If the middle edge is removed, the problem separates into components and one side has no fixed value unless another label is supplied. The nullspace theorem is therefore an identifiability condition for a prediction problem.

The regularised version makes the trade-off explicit. With observations on all vertices, minimise

12∥𝒙−𝒚∥22+τ2𝒙⊤L𝒙. \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2 +\frac{\tau}{2}\mathbf{x}^{\top}L\mathbf{x}.

The solution is (I+τL)−1𝒚(I+\tau L)^{-1}\mathbf{y}, so the Laplacian mode with eigenvalue λ\lambda is multiplied by 1/(1+τλ)1/(1+\tau\lambda). Low-frequency components survive and high-frequency components are attenuated. This connects graph-regularised regression directly to the filtering section and gives a diagnostic: if the desired signal is expected to change sharply across strong edges, the smoothness prior is structurally inappropriate rather than merely under-tuned.

The path example can be solved by hand. Label the two endpoints of P4P_4 with values 1 and 0, and let the two interior values be aa and bb. Harmonicity gives 2a−b=12a-b=1 and 2b−a=02b-a=0, so a=2/3a=2/3 and b=1/3b=1/3. The values interpolate linearly because every interior vertex averages its neighbours. If the middle edge receives weight ε\varepsilon, the equations change and the solution becomes less willing to transmit a label across the weak link. The exact formula is less important than the mechanism: edge weights control how strongly labels borrow information.

For classification, thresholding the harmonic scores introduces another error source. A score of 0.510.51 and a score of 0.990.99 can receive the same class label while representing different confidence under the graph model. A held-out loss should therefore be computed from the scores where possible, not only from hard labels. Calibration can also fail when a component has very few labels or when the graph contains a bridge that crosses a class boundary. The graph regulariser supplies a prior, not a probability model, unless a probabilistic observation model is added.

7.3 Ranking, Diffusion, and Information Flow

Random-walk and diffusion operators solve ranking problems by repeatedly redistributing mass through a graph. A restart or damping term prevents mass from circulating indefinitely and makes the linear system nonsingular. The result can rank pages, recommend items, prioritise proteins, or identify vertices reached quickly from a set of seeds. The spectral gap explains why some networks forget their starting set rapidly while a bottleneck preserves a local ranking for a long time.

The interpretation depends on what a step means. In a transport network a step might be a transition along a route; in a citation network it might be an abstract endorsement; in a recommendation graph it might be a similarity link. These are not interchangeable. A high-degree vertex receives large stationary mass under the standard walk, which may be desirable for exposure or may be an unwanted popularity bias. Degree normalisation, teleportation, and edge reweighting are choices about the ranking question, not merely implementation options.

Consider a seed set SS and an initial distribution concentrated on it. A short diffusion time answers a local question — which vertices are reached before the walk crosses a bottleneck — whereas a long time approaches the stationary distribution when the chain is connected and aperiodic. The same graph can therefore support a family of rankings indexed by time or restart strength. Reporting only the final ranking hides this scale choice. Plotting a few time points, or reporting the cumulative mass in the seed-side component, makes the effect of the spectral gap concrete.

For a restart walk, one common form is 𝒓t+1=αP⊤𝒓t+(1−α)𝒔\mathbf{r}_{t+1}=\alpha P^{\top}\mathbf{r}_t+(1-\alpha)\mathbf{s} for a seed distribution 𝒔\mathbf{s}. At equilibrium, (I−αP⊤)𝒓=(1−α)𝒔(I-\alpha P^{\top})\mathbf{r}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{s}. The parameter α\alpha is not merely a stabiliser: it specifies how far relevance is allowed to travel before the process returns to the seed. A large value emphasises global popularity and a small value emphasises local similarity. In an applied report, show sensitivity to α\alpha and explain which operational decision the chosen value represents.

The stationary distribution supplies a simple fairness warning. Under an undirected random walk, a vertex’s long-run mass is proportional to weighted degree. If degree reflects popularity, that may be the intended ranking. If degree reflects exposure, duplicated records, or unequal observation effort, the same ranking can amplify a measurement artefact. A restart distribution can make the score local, but it does not remove the need to audit degree semantics. Compare rankings under binary and count weights, and report rank changes for vertices whose degree is most affected by aggregation.

Diffusion time is another substantive parameter. At time zero, a seed score is completely local. At intermediate times, it follows paths whose lengths are controlled by the spectrum. At long times, it approaches the stationary or componentwise limit. A single equilibrium score can hide the speed and direction of spread that motivated diffusion. A useful worked result reports a short trajectory or a heat-kernel distance at several times, then explains which time scale corresponds to the application.

7.4 Images, Meshes, and Spatially Irregular Data

An image grid is a graph in which pixels are connected to nearby pixels, often with weights based on intensity similarity. A mesh graph connects vertices of a geometric discretisation. Spectral coordinates and diffusion then provide ways to denoise, segment, interpolate, or compare shapes without insisting on a rectangular ordering. The graph Laplacian is especially useful when the neighbourhood is irregular or when a surface has holes and varying degree.

The edge-weight rule controls whether an image boundary is preserved. If weights are high only between pixels with similar intensity, the energy penalises variation within a region more than across an edge. If weights are set solely by geometric distance, a sharp intensity boundary can be smoothed away. In either case, a spectral result should be interpreted as a property of the constructed graph, not as a property of the raw image independent of that construction.

7.5 Resilience, Redundancy, and Infrastructure

Effective resistance measures how much a network responds to a unit injection between two vertices. It is useful for assessing redundancy: a pair connected by many alternative paths has lower effective resistance than a pair joined by a single route, even when their shortest-path distance is the same. Electrical flows, random-walk commute times, and spanning-tree edge probabilities provide three ways to operationalise this idea.

In a power, communication, or transport network, this can guide the search for critical edges and candidate upgrades. It does not by itself model capacity, failure probabilities, congestion, or demand. A route edge with high effective resistance may be structurally important under the conductance model while carrying little real traffic. To make an infrastructure claim, combine the spectral diagnostic with a capacity or demand model and state the mapping between them.

The distinction between vulnerability and redundancy is easiest to see on three graphs with the same endpoints. A path has one available route, so its effective resistance is the sum of the edge resistances. A triangle has a direct route and an indirect route, so the two routes share the current and the resistance falls. A graph with many short routes can still have a high resistance if those routes all pass through one bridge. Shortest-path distance records one geodesic; effective resistance aggregates all routes through the energy-minimising flow. This is why resistance is useful as a screening statistic for network design, while it is not a substitute for a failure model.

Consider an infrastructure graph with two routes between a source and a sink. In the first graph the routes are disjoint; in the second they share one intermediate bridge. The shortest source-to-sink distance can be identical, but the second graph has higher effective resistance because one failure point carries all current between the sides. If a third parallel route is added, resistance falls. This makes resistance a natural feature for redundancy screening. It does not say which component will fail first, because failure probability and load are absent from the Laplacian model.

Spectral connectivity can also be used as a scenario comparison. Remove a candidate edge, recompute the relevant component count, algebraic connectivity, or resistance, and compare the change with the same operation on an alternative edge. The result ranks structural consequences under the declared weights. A resilience study should add demand-weighted or capacity-weighted scenarios when those are available, because a graph can be structurally resilient while operationally overloaded. A low spectral gap is a warning about a bottleneck; it is not a forecast of an outage.

If edge weights represent reliability rather than conductance, the electrical interpretation requires care. A reliability probability is not automatically additive under parallel and series composition, and transforming it into a conductance changes the quantity being modelled. The safe workflow is to state the transformation, use resistance as a structural feature under that transformation, and then test whether the feature improves a downstream reliability or demand model. The spectral calculation can suggest where to look; it cannot supply the missing operational semantics.

7.6 Scientific Networks and Multi-Scale Structure

In biological or neuroscience networks, vertices may be genes, brain regions, or species and edges may encode similarity, interaction, or co-occurrence. Low-frequency modes can reveal broad modules; higher modes can expose finer contrasts. Heat kernels and diffusion distances compare vertices across a chosen scale and can be less sensitive to indirect paths than shortest-path distance.

The danger is that correlation is not causation and an undirected similarity graph does not encode temporal direction. Spectral structure can be a useful descriptive compression or a feature for a downstream model, but it should not be presented as evidence of a mechanism without an additional identification argument. Reproducibility requires preserving the original data, graph construction, preprocessing, and operator convention, not only the final eigenvalues.

The spatial case also exposes the difference between geometric and signal smoothness. A kk-nearest-neighbour graph connects points that are close in coordinate space, while a kernel-weighted graph can weaken a geometrically close pair whose measured features differ sharply. On a synthetic two-region point cloud, heat diffusion on the distance graph crosses the boundary readily; the similarity-weighted graph preserves the boundary for longer because the cross-boundary edges have lower conductance. Neither result is “the” geometry of the data. Each is a consequence of a different prior about which local comparisons should be trusted.

For spatial meshes, the same scenario logic applies to discretisation choices. Compare a mesh Laplacian with and without a narrow bridge, a boundary connection, or a region of low conductance. If the first low mode changes dramatically under a refinement that should preserve the physical geometry, the discretisation or boundary condition needs investigation. If it changes as expected, the mode can be used as a reduced coordinate, but the reduction error should be checked against the original field or solution rather than inferred from eigenvalue ordering alone.

7.7 A Decision Checklist

Before choosing a spectral method, answer five questions:

  1. What does an edge weight mean, and should larger values strengthen or weaken coupling?
  2. Is the graph undirected, or is direction part of the phenomenon?
  3. Is the target exact connectivity, a balanced cut, diffusion, resistance, an embedding, or a numerical solve?
  4. Which vertices and components are scientifically in scope, including isolates?
  5. What observable quantity will be checked after the spectrum is computed?

If the answer to the last question is only “the eigenvectors look plausible”, the analysis is not yet specified. A conductance value, held-out prediction, residual, resistance calculation, or stability measure makes the spectral output answerable to the problem it was meant to solve.

The checklist can be turned into a compact method-selection map. Use a component count and the smallest Laplacian eigenvalues when the question is whether the network is connected or nearly separated. Use a normalised sweep when the question is a degree-aware bottleneck. Use several low modes when vertices need coordinates for clustering or visual comparison. Use heat or a lazy walk when the question concerns spread over a time scale. Use a grounded Laplacian solve when the question specifies injections, boundary values, or graph-regularised predictions. Use effective resistance when alternative routes, not one shortest route, are part of the problem.

Each choice has a matching validation object. Connectivity uses components and nullity. A cut uses a boundary ledger and conductance. An embedding uses subspace or downstream stability. Diffusion uses conservation and time trajectories. A linear solve uses residual and energy identities. Resistance uses endpoint symmetry and, where applicable, commute time. This pairing is more reliable than validating every method with the same generic eigenvalue printout.

The map also identifies when spectral methods are the wrong first tool. If direction is the phenomenon, preserve it and use a directed model. If negative edges encode antagonism, use a signed formulation. If the primary question is a single shortest route, Dijkstra-like methods are more direct. If edge weights are uncertain and the decision is a failure probability, combine spectral diagnostics with a stochastic reliability model. Spectral analysis is a family of relaxations and coordinates, not a universal replacement for graph algorithms or domain models.

8 Numerical Practice and Reproducible Computation

Build the operator, choose the numerical target, validate the result, and only then interpret or stress the output. Construction, normalisation, and component policy establish the problem before solver choice. The later guidance covers approximation and linear systems; failure diagnosis and twelve practice exercises then test the full operator contract.

8.1 Build the Operator Before Choosing the Algorithm

An eigensolver cannot repair a graph-construction error. Fix a vertex order and preserve it through the edge table, adjacency matrix, Laplacian, eigenvectors, and any plot. Audit whether repeated records represent parallel edges, duplicate observations of one relationship, or evidence that should be aggregated into a weight. Decide whether self-loops carry meaning. For the baseline loopless theory, remove or explicitly account for them rather than allowing a package’s default convention to decide silently. Similarly, a directed route table must not become an undirected graph merely because an undirected Laplacian is convenient.

For an undirected weighted graph, check symmetry and calculate weighted degrees from the same edge weights used in the off-diagonal entries. The basic identities are cheap and catch errors before an expensive decomposition:

L=L⊤,L𝟏=𝟎,tr⁡(L)=2∑e∈Ewe, L=L^{\top},\qquad L\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0},\qquad \operatorname{tr}(L)=2\sum_{e\in E}w_e,

and, for a test signal 𝒙\mathbf{x},

𝒙⊤L𝒙=∑{i,j}∈Ewij(xi−xj)2. \mathbf{x}^{\top}L\mathbf{x}= \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2.

The trace identity assumes that each undirected edge is counted once in the edge sum. If the input stores both orientations, aggregate or halve deliberately; do not apply the identity to an ambiguous edge table. A further useful check is that every off-diagonal non-zero in LL is non-positive for non-negative conductance weights, and that the row sums are zero up to floating-point round-off.

Dense storage has n2n^2 entries even when the graph has only m=O(n)m=O(n) edges. A dense double-precision matrix needs approximately 8n28n^2 bytes before workspace: n=10,000n=10,000 needs about 800 MB for one matrix, and a dense eigendecomposition usually needs additional working memory. Sparse storage represents the non-zeros and their indices, with storage proportional to n+mn+m for a simple graph. The practical crossover depends on the matrix format, hardware, and algorithm, but the conceptual rule is stable: sparse structure matters only if the computation preserves it.

8.2 Normalised and Unnormalised Operators Must Not Be Interchanged

The combinatorial Laplacian preserves the physical scale of the weights. Multiplying every conductance by cc multiplies LL and all its eigenvalues by cc. This is appropriate when weights represent conductance, capacity, or a count whose absolute magnitude matters. It also means that two graphs with the same topology but different measurement units have different combinatorial spectra.

The symmetric normalised Laplacian instead compares edge coupling with local degree:

ℒ=D†/2LD†/2=I−D†/2AD†/2 \mathcal{L}=D^{\dagger/2}LD^{\dagger/2} =I-D^{\dagger/2}AD^{\dagger/2}

on the positive-degree subspace. It is invariant to a global rescaling of all weights and has eigenvalues in [0,2][0,2] under the usual non-negative undirected assumptions. That makes it useful for degree-imbalanced graphs and for normalised-cut objectives, but it changes the geometry. A high-degree vertex is no longer allowed to dominate solely because it carries more incident weight.

The equivalent generalised eigenproblem is often the clearest statement of the distinction:

L𝒇=νD𝒇. L\mathbf{f}=\nu D\mathbf{f}.

The symmetric problem uses 𝒛=D1/2𝒇\mathbf{z}=D^{1/2}\mathbf{f}, so the vectors returned by an eigensolver for ℒ\mathcal{L} are not the same coordinates as the generalised eigenvectors 𝒇\mathbf{f}. In a spectral sweep, sorting fi=D−1/2zif_i=D^{-1/2}z_i is the relevant operation; sorting ziz_i directly can produce a different cut on an irregular graph. The random-walk operator I−PI-P is generally non-symmetric, but when all degrees are positive it is similar to ℒ\mathcal{L} and has the same eigenvalues. A symmetric solver is usually preferable when the symmetric representation is available.

In R, make the convention visible in the call. As of November 2026, the igraph Laplacian documentation describes normalization = "unnormalized", "symmetric", "left", and "right", and distinguishes the deprecated normalized argument. Do not rely on a default that is invisible in a report.

library(igraph)

vertices <- data.frame(name = as.character(1:5))
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("1", "2", "3"),
  to = c("2", "3", "4"),
  weight = c(1, 4, 1)
)
g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = FALSE, vertices = vertices)

L <- laplacian_matrix(
  g,
  weights = E(g)$weight,
  normalization = "unnormalized",
  sparse = FALSE
)
Lsym <- laplacian_matrix(
  g,
  weights = E(g)$weight,
  normalization = "symmetric",
  sparse = FALSE
)

stopifnot(max(abs(L - t(L))) < 1e-12)
stopifnot(max(abs(L %*% rep(1, vcount(g)))) < 1e-12)
eigen(L, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
eigen(Lsym, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values

This example is intentionally dense and small. It contains an isolate, so the package’s convention for the symmetric normalised operator must be checked before interpreting the zero eigenvalues. As of November 2026, the igraph Laplacian documentation describes the symmetric normalisation as I−D−1/2AD−1/2I-D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}, while this primer defines the isolated diagonal through the pseudoinverse convention. For positive-degree vertices the formulas agree; for isolates, state which convention was used and test it rather than assuming that two libraries count null vectors in the same way. The sparse = FALSE argument is also deliberate: base R’s eigen() expects a dense matrix, and converting a large graph this way defeats sparse storage.

8.3 Disconnected Graphs and Isolated Vertices Need a Policy

For the combinatorial Laplacian, the multiplicity of zero is the number of connected components, including singleton isolated vertices. A solver returning several values near zero is not necessarily failing; it may be revealing disconnected structure or a weak bridge. Conversely, a tiny positive value does not prove disconnection. A bridge of weight 10−1210^{-12} keeps the mathematical graph connected, although its algebraic connectivity can be below a practical tolerance.

Start with graph components, not eigenvalues. Record the number of components and their sizes, identify isolates, and decide whether the scientific question concerns the full graph or each non-trivial component. If a spectral embedding is intended to describe one connected population, compute it component by component or select the relevant component explicitly. If an isolate represents a meaningful observation, retain it and report that it has no edge-based coordinate information. Removing it is a modelling decision, not a numerical clean-up.

The normalised case is more delicate because D−1D^{-1} is undefined at degree zero. Three policies are common: remove isolates for a walk-based analysis; define inverse degree entries as zero and use a zero row and column in the symmetric operator; or use an identity-based convention that places a one on an isolated diagonal. These choices produce different nullities and different embeddings. None should be hidden inside a convenience function. The random-walk matrix also needs a policy for zero-degree rows; a row of zeros is not stochastic, while assigning a self-loop changes the model.

Laplacian solves expose the same structure. The equation L𝒗=𝒃L\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b} has a solution only when the injection vector sums to zero on every connected component. Potentials are non-unique because adding a componentwise constant changes nothing. An isolate has a zero row; it cannot absorb a non-zero injection. Check compatibility before calling a solver, and either ground one vertex in each relevant component or work in the orthogonal complement of the nullspace. Silently adding a small diagonal ridge makes a nonsingular system, but it also changes the physical problem.

8.4 Dense and Sparse Eigensolvers Answer Different Computational Questions

For a small or moderately sized symmetric matrix, a dense symmetric eigensolver is the simplest reference method. It computes the full spectrum and an orthonormal basis, normally through a LAPACK routine. That is valuable when you need all modes, when you are testing a new graph construction, or when you need a trusted answer against which to compare an iterative method. The cost is typically cubic in nn and the storage is quadratic. It is not a sensible default merely because a graph has a convenient adjacency matrix.

For a large sparse Laplacian, the usual question is narrower: obtain the first few non-zero eigenpairs, or obtain a few eigenvectors near a selected spectral region. Lanczos-type methods, including ARPACK implementations, use matrix-vector products and do not need to store every dense entry. A sparse multiplication with LL costs roughly O(m)O(m) for a graph with mm edges. The total cost depends on the requested number of eigenpairs, eigenvalue separation, reorthogonalisation, stopping tolerance, and the cost of the sparse linear solves used by some modes. It is therefore misleading to promise that a sparse eigensolver costs only O(m)O(m): that is the cost of one multiplication, not the whole convergence process.

The smallest eigenvalues are often the difficult ones. Lanczos convergence is governed by spectral separation, and a cluster of nearly equal eigenvalues can require many iterations. Shift-invert methods transform the problem so that eigenvalues near a shift become dominant, but each iteration then requires solving a system involving L−σIL-\sigma I. For a Laplacian, a shift can make the system nonsingular, but factorisation may introduce fill-in and consume much more memory than the original graph. A preconditioned locally optimal block method can be preferable when several close eigenvalues are required, provided that a good preconditioner is available.

The choice should follow the output, not the package name. Use a dense method when you need the complete small spectrum or a diagnostic reference. Use a sparse iterative method when nn is large, the graph is genuinely sparse, and only a small number of modes is required. Use an operator callback when forming even a sparse matrix is inconvenient, but retain an independent way to evaluate residuals. If a method is asked for a Fiedler vector, make sure it is seeking the second-smallest eigenvalue rather than the eigenvalue of largest magnitude. For a normalised Laplacian, the spectrum lies in a bounded interval, while the combinatorial spectrum scales with the weights and can have a very different numerical range.

There is a practical indexing trap in “the first few eigenpairs”. If a graph has cc components, the combinatorial Laplacian has cc zero modes, so the first non-trivial mode is at index c+1c+1 in one-based ascending order. A nearly disconnected graph has one exact zero and a small positive mode instead. Asking an iterative routine for two smallest eigenvalues and then taking the second column can consequently return a component indicator, a weak-bridge mode, or a vector in a nearly repeated nullspace. Compute components first and specify whether the target is the first positive eigenvalue, the first non-zero eigenvalue above a tolerance, or a fixed index.

Shift-invert methods deserve a separate caution. Transforming Mq=λqM q=\lambda q around a shift σ\sigma makes eigenvalues near σ\sigma easier to find by applying (M−σI)−1(M-\sigma I)^{-1}. For a Laplacian, this requires repeated linear solves and can destroy the memory advantage if a factorisation fills in. A shift just above zero can separate small positive modes from the bulk, but it also interacts with exact nullspaces and component policies. The method is powerful when the factorisation is affordable, not a universal upgrade over ordinary Lanczos iterations.

For a large graph, a matrix-free implementation can apply the Laplacian without assembling AA or DD. Given an edge list, one matrix-vector product can accumulate we(xi−xj)w_e(x_i-x_j) at each endpoint. This makes the O(m)O(m) structure explicit and is often useful for heat-kernel or Krylov calculations. It also removes some convenient invariant checks, so retain a smaller assembled operator or periodically compare the callback against a sparse matrix on random test vectors. Matrix-free is a storage strategy, not permission to omit validation.

Repeated and nearly repeated eigenvalues change what can be validated. A solver may return a different orthonormal basis for the same eigenspace on two runs, even when both results are correct. Comparing columns one by one then reports a false discrepancy. Compare the projectors QQ⊤QQ^{\top}, principal angles, or the residual of the whole invariant subspace. Eigenvector signs are arbitrary even for a simple eigenvalue; orienting a vector by making its largest-magnitude entry positive is a display convention, not a mathematical correction.

8.5 Convergence and Validation Are Part of the Result

An eigensolver’s “converged” flag is evidence about its internal stopping rule, not a proof that the intended graph and operator were used. For an approximate eigenpair (λ̂,q̂)(\widehat{\lambda},\widehat{q}), compute the residual
